name: Cold-pressed oils / olive oil

image.caption: Salt, olive oil, vinegar - Hellenic Republic

lead: Cold-pressed oils, most prominently extra virgin olive oil, are extracted mechanically without heat or solvents. People in looksmaxxing and diet circles use them in place of refined seed oils, linking them to healthier skin and general health.

The oil is rich in oleic acid and polyphenols. In the US the FDA allows a qualified health claim that limited and not conclusive evidence suggests about two tablespoons daily may reduce coronary heart disease risk when replacing saturated fat; effects on appearance have not been established.

paras: People use extra virgin olive oil for dressings, finishing and low-to-medium heat cooking, and swap it in for seed oils. Because its polyphenols are sensitive to heat, light and oxygen, it is usually stored dark and cool.
Few direct risks are reported. Documented concerns involve fraud and mislabelling in the olive oil market, and the FDA claim is described as limited and not conclusive.

chain: Swap seed oils for olive oil
Different fatty acid and polyphenol intake
angle.text: Looksmaxxers use extra virgin olive oil and other cold-pressed oils in place of refined seed oils, citing skin and general health. Swapping oils changes fatty acid and polyphenol intake, which is the route people credit for healthier skin. Olive oil has regulator-qualified heart-health claims; appearance effects have not been tested.

lead: Cold-pressed oils, most prominently extra virgin olive oil, are edible oils extracted mechanically without heat or chemical solvents. In looksmaxxing and wider diet-culture discussion they are used as the cooking and finishing fat in place of refined seed oils, with followers hoping for clearer skin, a leaner physique and better general health, and some also use olive oil as a calorie-dense way to add food intake while bulking [1][2][3].

The appearance chain people describe runs from swapping refined seed oils for olive oil, to a diet richer in oleic acid and polyphenols, to better-conditioned skin and body composition. Olive oil also has a long cosmetic history, from Greek athletes rubbing it on the body to modern use as a skin moisturiser and hair oil, and some looksmaxxers apply it directly [1].

Extra virgin olive oil is the top grade under International Olive Council standards, requiring mechanical extraction and free acidity of no more than 0.8 percent [1]. In the US the FDA allows a qualified health claim that limited and not conclusive evidence suggests about two tablespoons daily may reduce coronary heart disease risk when replacing saturated fat [1].

Research centres on cardiovascular and metabolic outcomes: an umbrella review of vegetable oils associated virgin olive oil, canola and rice bran oils with lower total and LDL cholesterol, and a meta-analysis of cohorts and trials linked olive oil intake to lower cardiovascular risk [4][5]. Public-health bodies and nutrition scientists, by contrast, describe the wider claims that seed oils are harmful as not supported by evidence, a debate that has driven much of the online interest in cold-pressed oils [6].

About 2.74 million tonnes in 2022; Spain about 24% [1]
FDA qualified claim (heart disease); EFSA 2011 claims on polyphenols and LDL [1]

paras: Virgin oils are made by mechanical means only, without solvents or refining; extra virgin oil must also have no more than 0.8 percent free acidity and no significant sensory defects, while virgin oil allows up to 2 percent [1]. Cold pressed generally means the oil was not heated above about 25 to 27 degrees Celsius, though the EU reserves that term for oil that is physically pressed rather than centrifuged, which must be labelled cold extracted, and the phrase first cold pressed has no reliable international definition [1].

Production involves crushing olives, malaxing the paste so droplets join, separating oil from water by pressing or centrifuge, and optional filtering. Refined and pomace oils involve chemical processing or solvents [1]. The International Olive Council governs about 95 percent of international production, the USDA adopted voluntary grading standards in 2010, and California made its standards mandatory for large producers in 2014 [1].

Olive oil is mostly monounsaturated oleic acid (55 to 83 percent), with smaller amounts of linoleic acid (3.5 to 21 percent) and palmitic acid (7.5 to 20 percent) [1]. Polyphenols make up about 0.5 percent, including oleuropein, oleocanthal and hydroxytyrosol, and give the bitter, peppery taste; vitamin E is also present [1]. Heat, prolonged storage and oxygen degrade polyphenols, and early harvesting, cold extraction and dark, cool storage help preserve them [1]. Reviews describe olive polyphenols as having antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties [7].

Neolithic people collected wild olives in Asia Minor by the 8th millennium BC, and archaeological finds in Galilee and near Haifa show oil production between about 6000 and 4500 BC [1]. Egypt imported oil before 2000 BC, Mycenaean Greece exported it around 1450 to 1150 BC, and the Romans spread olive farming across the Mediterranean [1]. Joseph Graham's hydraulic press of 1795 improved productivity, and olive trees reached the Americas in the 16th century [1].

Olive oil's modern dietary profile owes much to the Mediterranean diet, publicised in 1975 by Ancel and Margaret Keys after their Seven Countries Study, which was published in 1970, and later supported by US and international dietary bodies [8]. Spain produced about 24 percent of the world's roughly 2.74 million tonnes in 2022, followed by Italy, Greece, Turkey and Tunisia [1].

In 2011 the European Food Safety Authority supported claims that olive polyphenols protect blood lipids from oxidation and that replacing saturated fat with oleic acid helps maintain normal LDL cholesterol, but said cause and effect was not established for triglycerides, HDL cholesterol or blood glucose [1].

The Mediterranean diet, in which olive oil is the main fat, has been associated in reviews with lower cardiovascular risk and other outcomes, though a 2019 Cochrane review described the benefits as modest and of low-to-moderate certainty [8]. Wikipedia reports that a 2014 meta-analysis linked higher olive oil intake with lower all-cause mortality, cardiovascular events and stroke [8].

Seed oils are a recurring theme in ancestral-diet and carnivore-diet circles, and cold-pressed olive oil is often named as the preferred alternative. Wikipedia traces the oils criticised to early 20th-century industrialisation, such as Procter and Gamble's cottonseed-based Crisco in 1911, and notes critics' objections to solvent extraction and to omega-6 content [6]. It names Paul Saladino's 2020 appearance on the Joe Rogan Experience, Cate Shanahan's 'hateful eight' phrase and later statements by public figures including Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in 2024 as moments in the claim's spread [6].

The same article reports that Harvard's public health school, the American Heart Association and cancer organisations have said the evidence does not show seed oils to be harmful, including a 2009 AHA advisory that reducing omega-6 intake would be more likely to raise than lower coronary heart disease risk, and a 2019 pooled analysis linking higher circulating linoleic acid with lower cardiovascular risk [6]. Proponents of avoidance disagree and point to processing and the omega-6 to omega-3 ratio [6].

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and diet communities
paras: On looksmax.org, olive oil appears mainly in diet threads, for example a member asking how to use it to add calories for bulking without ruining the face or body; a reply notes that extra calories from any source add body fat that can be lost later in a deficit, and another gives a rule of thumb of about 1 g of lipids per kg of bodyweight [2]. T Nation forum members have likewise discussed olive oil as a calorie source for a teenage athlete struggling to reach a high calorie target on a Paleolithic-style diet [3].

Opinions in older T Nation threads differ on whether to use it: one member advocated extra-virgin cold-pressed olive oil for low-heat cooking, while another said he preferred other cold-pressed organic oils because olive oil goes rancid quickly and its health effects from small amounts are negligible [9][10]. Proponents of seed-oil avoidance regard cold-pressed olive oil as a cleaner alternative, a view not directly tested for appearance outcomes.

Wikipedia notes that olive oil has long been used in skincare, cosmetics and soaps, and that the ancient Spartans and other Greeks rubbed it on their bodies during exercise [1]. In a 2013 randomized study of 19 adult volunteers, researchers compared olive oil and sunflower seed oil applied to forearm skin and measured the effect on skin barrier properties; the study was framed around neonatal skin care practice [11]. The investigators noted that the practice of using natural oils on skin was widespread but lacked supporting evidence [11].

Journalist Tom Mueller's 2011 book Extra Virginity, which expanded on his 2007 New Yorker article Slippery Business, argued that the global olive oil industry suffers from fraud and weak regulation, and that defective oil is often altered and sold as extra virgin; it also criticised the International Olive Council [12]. Reviews of the book were mixed, with Kirkus positive and the New York Times critical of the prose [12].

Authorities have run enforcement operations since: in 2008 Operation Golden Oil in Italy involved 23 arrests, and in 2012 Spanish authorities arrested 19 people in a scheme passing off other oils as Italian olive oil [1]. In 2017 Italian police arrested 33 suspects over mislabelled pomace oil exported as extra virgin, and in July 2024 the EU reported a record number of olive oil fraud incidents [1].

An umbrella review of 48 studies and 206 meta-analyses reported that virgin olive oil, canola and rice bran oils were associated with lower total cholesterol and LDL concentrations, with certainty ranging from moderate to very low [4]. A 2022 meta-analysis of 24 prospective cohorts and randomized-trial reports covering several hundred thousand participants per outcome found a 16 percent lower cardiovascular risk for each additional 25 g per day of olive oil [5]. The CORDIOPREV trial of 1,002 coronary patients and the PREDIMED trial tested Mediterranean diets rich in extra virgin olive oil in cardiovascular settings [13][14]. A randomized comparison of coconut oil, olive oil and butter measured blood lipids and cardiovascular risk factors in healthy adults [15].

For appearance, a 2013 randomized forearm trial of 19 adults examined olive oil on the adult skin barrier [11]. No studies were found on cold-pressed oils as a seed-oil replacement for appearance outcomes.
